title: Bit-plane segmented KV cache with attention-gated plane residency
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: split every FP16 KV vector into a high plane (sign, exponent, top mantissa bits) and a low-mantissa plane stored in separate pages; only high planes stay in HBM, low planes live in CXL/LPDDR or NVMe and are fetched only for tokens whose coarse attention score (computed from high planes alone) lands in the top-k. Resolves 'keep all context' vs 'keep little memory' by holding every token coarsely and few tokens fully, losslessly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context serving memory; ~2-3x less HBM per session with a lossless fallback, so fewer HBM stacks (HBM TSV tax, cost/bit).

title: Controller-side pointer high-bit extraction into per-page region tags
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: the memory controller detects 64-bit words whose upper 24 bits equal a per-page 'region tag' (pointers into the same heap region), strips those bits and packs eight 40-bit pointers into a 40-byte slot, restoring them on read with one mux stage. It is hardware compressed-oops for every language, not just the JVM.
why: Pointer-heavy heaps (graph DBs, Go/Java, kernels, B-trees) are 30-60% pointers; 20-35% capacity gain on those pages at ~1-cycle decode.

title: Trust-domain-salted dedup with constant-time copy-on-write
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: instead of fleet-wide page dedup (switched off after Flip-Feng-Shui and timing side channels), salt dedup fingerprints per trust domain so pages merge only inside one tenant, and route every write to a mergeable page through the same constant-latency CoW path whether shared or not. Each region gets its own dedup policy instead of one global on/off switch.
why: Resolves 'dedup saves memory vs dedup leaks information'; recovers 10-30% capacity on VM/container hosts where dedup is disabled today.

title: Encode-heavy, decode-cheap memory codec trained by idle cores
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: reads outnumber writes ~3-10x, so use an asymmetric codec: pages are written raw, then idle cores or a background engine re-encode warm pages with expensive search (optimal parsing plus per-page tANS tables), while the read path is a fixed two-stage table-lookup decoder with deterministic ~10 ns latency.
why: Gets entropy-coder ratios (2.5-3.5x) at BDI-class read latency on warm data; 1.5-2x effective DRAM on read-mostly working sets.

title: Fuzzy cross-request KV merging with sparse residual patches
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: beyond exact prefix sharing, the serving engine clusters KV blocks from concurrent requests whose vectors differ by less than epsilon (same retrieved chunks at different offsets after RoPE de-rotation, templated prompts) and stores one canonical block plus a sparse INT4 residual per request. A radix tree keyed on locality-sensitive hashes finds merge candidates.
why: RAG and agent workloads re-ingest the same chunks at varying positions where exact prefix caching misses; 2-5x KV memory reduction in multi-tenant serving.

title: ECC check bits double as free dedup fingerprints
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: the controller already computes SECDED/Chipkill check bytes for every 64 B line it writes; concatenating a page's check words yields a 512-byte signature that serves as a near-free dedup/similarity fingerprint, kept incrementally in a small on-chip table and byte-verified on a hit, so no CPU hashing or KSM-style scanning is needed.
why: Dedup is often disabled because hashing and scanning cost CPU and bandwidth; making it ~free recovers 5-25% of VM-host DRAM.

title: Matryoshka weight residency: MSB nest in DRAM, residual off-board
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: quantize weights with nested codebooks so the 4-bit code is literally the top nibble of the 8-bit code; DRAM/HBM holds only the 4-bit nest while the residual nibble sits in CXL memory or flash and is streamed per layer only when a cheap per-token confidence probe says that layer needs full precision.
why: Halves weight memory in the common case while keeping an INT8 quality ceiling; 1.6-2x capacity for weight-bound inference.

title: Layer-stride KV checkpoints recomputed by idle tensor cores
idea: TRIZ #8 Counterweight: balance scarce memory with abundant FLOPs by storing the residual-stream hidden state only every Nth layer (e.g., N=4) for cold tokens and recomputing the intermediate layers' K/V on demand during decode, using the tensor-core slack that memory-bound decode leaves idle.
why: Decode runs at 10-30% compute utilization; spending that slack cuts cold-context KV memory ~3-4x with modest added latency.

title: Producer-side compression: NICs and SSDs write memory pre-compressed
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: publish the memory controller's compressed-line format as a standard and let NICs, SSD controllers and accelerators DMA data already in that format, so the uncompressed copy never occupies DRAM; the CPU's controller decompresses only when a core actually touches the line.
why: I/O buffers, page cache and receive rings are 10-30% of server DRAM; storing them compressed from birth gives ~1.5-2x on that slice and saves write bandwidth.

title: Binaries ship heap-trained compression dictionaries loaded at context switch
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: at build/profile time, train a 4-16 KB dictionary on representative heap snapshots of each application and embed it in the ELF; the OS loads it into a dictionary slot in the memory controller on context switch, so line-granular compression is application-specific from the first write.
why: Generic line compressors reach ~1.3-1.6x; app-trained dictionaries give 2-3x on structured heaps (protobufs, JSON, strings).

title: Provision DRAM at median compression ratio with emergency spill tier
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: size each server's physical DRAM for the median, not worst-case, compression ratio and pre-install a cushion (a small battery-backed NAND-on-CXL tier plus a pinned 3% reserve) that absorbs a ratio collapse instantly while the scheduler migrates the offending workload away.
why: Operators provision for worst case and throw away the compression win; cushioning lets 30-50% less DRAM be bought for the same virtual capacity.

title: Anti-correlated memory-peak co-scheduling across a cluster
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: profile each job's memory-over-time curve and bin-pack jobs whose peaks are anti-correlated (phase-shifted GC cycles, batch vs interactive, prefill vs decode) onto the same host, so hosts are sized for the peak of the sum instead of the sum of peaks; memory stays 'level' instead of every host being lifted to peak.
why: Fleet DRAM is sized to peaks while average use is 40-60%; 15-30% fleet DRAM reduction.

title: Client-held encrypted session state for idle conversations
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of the server holding idle users' KV cache, ship a compressed (low-rank plus INT4), encrypted, integrity-tagged KV snapshot to the user's device after each turn and have the client return it with the next request; servers keep KV only for sessions that are generating right now.
why: Most chat sessions are idle >95% of wall time; moving idle KV onto client devices cuts server KV residency by roughly an order of magnitude for long-context chat.

title: Spherical-coordinate quantization of keys and embeddings
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: convert key and embedding vectors from Cartesian to recursive polar form (one norm plus d-1 angles); after a random rotation the angles are tightly concentrated, so they quantize to 2-3 bits with no per-block scale or zero-point metadata.
why: Removes quantization metadata and outlier handling; ~4-6x KV/embedding compression vs FP16 at near-lossless attention fidelity.

title: Live-morphing data structures between dense and succinct forms
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: runtime libraries let every hash map, vector and index switch representation online, morphing cold instances into succinct forms (Elias-Fano, rank/select bitvectors, minimal perfect hashes) and expanding hot ones back to pointer-rich forms, driven by sampled access counts.
why: Much in-memory data is cold but must stay in DRAM; succinct forms are 3-10x smaller, giving 1.5-2.5x heap reduction in data-heavy services.

title: Key-only residency: values fetched from flash for top-k tokens
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: keep only the quantized keys of long contexts in HBM, because keys decide where attention goes, and leave values on NVMe/CXL; after scoring, fetch values only for the top-k attended tokens (typically 1-5%) with batched reads.
why: Values are half the KV footprint and sparse attention touches few of them; ~2x KV HBM reduction with bounded flash bandwidth.

title: Frequency-domain storage of activation tensors
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: store saved activations and feature maps after a blockwise DCT/Hadamard transform with truncated high-frequency coefficients, since smooth tensors concentrate energy in few coefficients; the inverse transform is fused into the consuming kernel.
why: Training activation memory and vision/video feature caches compress 3-6x, cutting HBM capacity per accelerator.

title: Typing-indicator-timed KV swap synchronized to user think time
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: chat traffic has a rhythm of generation followed by 10-120 s of reading and typing; page each session's KV to flash the moment generation ends and start prefetching it back when the client reports the first keystroke, hiding the swap inside human latency.
why: Turns idle-session KV, most of the resident set, into flash-resident data; 3-10x less HBM/DRAM per concurrent user.

title: Time-multiplex accelerator HBM between inference peaks and training troughs
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: the same HBM pool hosts serving KV caches at diurnal peaks and fine-tuning/eval activations at night, with sub-minute handoff via sharded checkpoints to CXL/flash, so no byte sits idle 12 hours a day.
why: Inference fleets average ~30-50% memory use; shrinks the separate training-memory fleet by 20-40%.

title: Cache-resident streaming rings that skip DRAM entirely
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping: NICs and SSDs inject data into an LLC-pinned ring (DDIO-style) whose credit-based flow control is matched to the consumer's processing rate, so streaming data is consumed and dropped before it is ever written back to DRAM.
why: Streaming analytics, packet processing and ETL hold large DRAM buffers only as staging; 5-10x smaller buffers and less write bandwidth.

title: Train models with KV-dropout so memory starvation is harmless
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: inject random KV eviction (drop 30-70% of past tokens' KV, biased toward older ones) as a regularizer during pre- and post-training, turning the harm of missing context into learned robustness so inference can evict aggressively with negligible quality loss.
why: KV eviction degrades unadapted models; evictability-trained models could run at 2-4x smaller KV budgets.

title: Refresh-piggybacked in-situ recompression by the memory logic die
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: DRAM must open every row each refresh window anyway; the HBM/CXL logic die issues column reads into rows already opened for refresh to scan, dedup-fingerprint and recompress cold pages, so compaction rides on maintenance activations instead of adding its own.
why: Turns refresh (16-33% of idle power) into useful work; continuous compaction at near-zero added activation energy, enabling 1.3-2x effective capacity.

title: Seed-regenerated tensors replace stored random matrices
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: replace stored pseudo-random data (random projections, sketch matrices, hash tables, dropout masks, random-feature kernels) by a seed plus a counter-based PRNG (Philox-style) unit near memory that regenerates any element on access, a perfect copy that costs no bits.
why: Sketching and random-projection-heavy models can hold GBs of pseudo-random tensors; removes that slice entirely at small compute cost.

title: Per-package 180 nm companion die doing wide-slow line compression
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: instead of one fast advanced-node compression engine, wire-bond a cheap 180 nm companion die beside each DRAM die in the package; each handles only its own chip's x8 slice with a 256-bit-wide internal datapath at 100-200 MHz running BDI/FPC compression, so segmentation makes slow old silicon fast enough.
why: Adds transparent 1.4-2x line compression to commodity modules using fully depreciated 200 mm fabs, with no advanced-node controller redesign.

title: PCI-class hardware RAM Doubler card for cold pages
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: take compression out of the latency path entirely; a 180 nm bus-master card (PCI-X/PCIe gen1 class, ~1 GB/s) compresses only pages idle >1 s with an LZ-class engine and packs them into a compressed DRAM pool, which the OS uses like zswap with hardware offload, echoing 1996's RAM Doubler.
why: Cold-page churn is ~10-100 MB/s per server, well within 1990s bandwidth; 20-40% more effective DRAM with no CPU cycles spent.

title: Precision-transcoding DIMM buffer for tagged ML address ranges
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: a 180 nm buffer chip on the module holds a small range table; writes to tagged ranges are converted FP32 to BF16 or FP16 to FP8 with stochastic rounding and stored packed into a half- or quarter-size physical region, and reads are expanded back, so precision varies by region with no software changes.
why: CPU-side ML data (embeddings, optimizer state, feature stores) is often FP32; 2-4x capacity on those ranges using simple 180 nm arithmetic.

title: Multi-port read-only shared pool for rack-wide weights and images
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: split memory into an asymmetric write-rarely class (model weights, OS images, libraries, reference data) held once per rack in a multi-ported 180 nm memory controller with 16 slow, wide ports, like 1990s dual-port VRAM or mainframe shared storage, while each server keeps only small private read-write DRAM.
why: Every server today holds its own copy of identical read-only data; removing 16 duplicates shrinks that slice ~16x, often 15-40% of server DRAM.

title: Near-DIMM dequantize-and-pool engine for embedding tables
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: merge the gather, dequantize and sum-pool steps of recommendation embedding lookups into a 180 nm logic chip on the module buffer; rows are stored as 4-bit codes with a per-row scale, and the chip expands and pools them locally, returning one FP16 vector per lookup bag.
why: Embedding tables are TB-scale and dominate recommender DRAM; in-place dequant makes 4-bit storage practical (~4x capacity) and cuts channel traffic 10-50x.

title: 640K-style memory budgets enforced in CI and procurement
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: stop bloat before it ships; every service declares bytes-per-request and bytes-per-session budgets that CI heap profilers check (a regression fails the build), and public procurement scores bids on measured DRAM per transaction, much as 1990s developers lived within 640 KB.
why: Software memory bloat grows demand ~20%/yr; budgets need zero new silicon and could cut fleet demand growth by about a third.

title: Copper-style overlay sequencer streaming model layers from parallel flash
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: a compiler precomputes a full 1980s-style overlay schedule of which weight tiles are needed when, and a 180 nm microcoded DMA sequencer (like the Amiga Copper) executes it, streaming tiles from 16-32 parallel NAND channels into a small DRAM ring one or two layers ahead of compute.
why: Deterministic batch inference needs only ~2 layers resident; 5-20x less weight DRAM, using only old-node control logic.

title: Bank-switched DIMM capacity reassigned between hosts by analog muxes
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: like EMS bank switching, a pool box of memory modules sits behind passive analog crossbar switches buildable on old processes; at millisecond-to-minute granularity a controller quiesces a module group and re-routes it from one host's channel to another's, with OS memory hot-plug onlining and offlining it.
why: Stranded DRAM is 10-25% in clouds; physical reassignment without CXL-class SerDes lets racks buy ~15% less DRAM.

title: Deterministic lockstep replay replaces resident state for idle actors
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: store idle entities (game objects, agents, session actors, simulation cells) in the time dimension, keeping only their input event log since the last checkpoint, and regenerate state by deterministic replay when touched, the way 1997-era RTS games synchronized by inputs only.
why: Idle actor state is often 60-90% of resident memory in stateful backends and logs are 10-100x smaller than state; needs no new hardware.

title: Follow-the-moon placement of memory-hungry jobs across regions
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: route memory-heavy batch work (long-context KV-heavy jobs, analytics, fine-tuning) to whichever regions are in their nightly interactive trough, so each region's DRAM is sized for the global average instead of its own daytime peak plus batch.
why: Diurnal peak-to-trough ratios of 2-3x mean 20-35% less global DRAM; needs only schedulers and existing networks.

title: Lisp-machine-style hardware GC tracer beside the memory controller
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: burn garbage faster with a 180 nm tracing coprocessor next to memory (like the Symbolics and TI Explorer GC assists) that marks reachable objects in parallel at memory bandwidth using tag bits, so managed runtimes collect continuously and run heaps at ~1.2x live size instead of the usual 2-3x.
why: Java/Go/JS/Python fleets spend 40-60% of heap DRAM on GC headroom; tracing is memory-bound, so old-node logic is fast enough.

title: Output-entropy-gated KV precision on existing hardware
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: the serving loop watches each request's next-token entropy; while the model is confident, new KV is stored at INT2-INT3, and when entropy spikes it switches to INT8 and re-quantizes recent blocks, a closed loop that spends bits only where uncertainty demands. It runs as software on hardware already deployed.
why: Average KV width drops from 16 bits to ~3 bits with a quality guard; ~4-5x KV capacity, no new silicon.

title: 180 nm TCAM dedup engine for constant-time page fingerprint lookup
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: borrow the 1990s router TCAM; a 180 nm ternary CAM holds partial fingerprints of pages, each newly written or newly cold page is looked up in one cycle, and only hits are byte-verified, making dedup a continuous hardware service instead of a CPU scan.
why: KSM-style scanning costs CPU and finds duplicates late; continuous dedup recovers 10-30% of memory in VM/container hosts.

title: Self-describing paired lines with header-in-slack, no metadata table
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: when two adjacent 64 B lines each compress to 30 B or less, they are packed into one 64 B slot whose first bits describe the encoding, and the freed buddy slot goes to a free list; a decoder simple enough for 180 nm reads the header in-line, so no separate metadata table, metadata cache or extra DRAM access is needed.
why: Removes the metadata-access penalty that kills line compression; 1.3-1.8x capacity with decode logic small enough for old nodes.

title: Retired-DIMM far-memory sleds behind 180 nm bridge controllers
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: harvest DDR3/DDR4 modules from decommissioned servers into sleds run at derated speed (DDR3-800 class) by 180 nm bridge controllers with ~3 Gb/s SerDes, exposing them as a compressed far-memory tier for cold pages.
why: Millions of retired modules are shredded every year; reuse adds nearly free capacity and offsets 10-20% of new DRAM purchases with no new advanced-node silicon.

title: 180 nm silicon-photonic links for rack-scale memory pooling
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution: replace copper memory links with optical ones built on 200 mm, 180 nm photonics lines (ring modulators and Ge photodiodes need no fine lithography), giving accelerators reach to a shared memory pool with only tens of ns of flight time, so each carries less local HBM.
why: Copper reach limits force per-device HBM; pooling cuts provisioned capacity 20-40% and the number of HBM stacks.

title: Sampling working-set monitor chip that shrink-wraps container limits
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells: a 180 nm chip on the module samples 1-in-1024 accesses into a count-min sketch per 2 MB region and reports true working sets, letting the OS shrink each container's memory 'shell' to fit and reclaim the remainder to compressed or far tiers.
why: Containers are over-provisioned 30-50%; accurate hardware working-set data supports 20-30% reclaim without performance cliffs.

title: Porous page mapping backs only written 256-byte chunks
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: a 180 nm memory-side translation chip makes each 4 KB (or 2 MB huge) page 'porous'; only the 256 B chunks actually written get physical backing, tracked by a per-page 16-bit occupancy mask, and unwritten holes read as zero and cost nothing.
why: Internal fragmentation and huge-page bloat waste 10-30% of DRAM in sparse heaps and hash tables; recovered with no software changes.

title: RAMDAC-style palettized tensors decoded by near-memory lookup tables
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes: as 1990s VGA stored 8-bit palette indices instead of 24-bit color, store weights and embeddings as 3-4-bit indices into per-tensor 8-16-entry palettes learned by k-means; a 180 nm RAMDAC-like LUT chip on the memory path expands indices to FP16 on read.
why: 4-5x weight/embedding capacity vs FP16, with non-uniform levels that beat uniform INT4 accuracy and trivial decode logic.

title: Hash-consing allocator merges identical immutable objects at birth
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: the language runtime interns every immutable object (strings, tuples, small records, JSON subtrees) through a hash table at allocation, so identical values become one physical object, as 1990s Lisp and ML systems did; it runs on any CPU.
why: Duplicate objects are 10-40% of heaps in data-processing services, and object-level dedup is far finer than page dedup.

title: Erasure-coded in-memory stores replace triple replication
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: discard replicas and recover lost data from parity; in-memory caches and KV stores stripe objects RS(8,2) across servers' DRAM, with encode and decode done at line rate by a 180 nm XOR/Galois-field engine on the NIC.
why: 3x replication becomes 1.25x overhead, a ~58% DRAM saving for replicated in-memory datasets.

title: Segment:offset 32-bit relative pointers for in-memory data structures
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: like 8086 segment:offset addressing, data structures store 32-bit (or 16-bit) offsets relative to a segment base held in FS/GS or a register, inside 4 GB arenas, halving pointer width; compilers emit base-plus-offset loads at ~1 cycle of cost.
why: Pointers are 30-50% of graph, tree and object heaps; 15-30% total heap reduction on existing CPUs.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM freezes model weights into old-node silicon
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: freeze 'liquid' read-only weights into 'solid' via-programmed NOR/NAND mask ROM on 180 nm lines, where only one via mask changes per model, so frozen weights and vocabulary tables leave DRAM for cheap, refresh-free, one-transistor-per-bit storage.
why: Removes read-only data from DRAM for edge and embedded inference with zero refresh and cheap masks (~$20-50k); density of ~0.1-0.2 GB/cm2 limits it to small models.
